````math
## Appendix E Analysis of Evaluation Metrics

### E.1. LLM-as-a-judge

It is worth noting that LLM-as-a-judge evaluation is not perfectly
reliable, as its results may be affected by the capability of the judge
model, the evaluation prompt, and other factors ([Zheng et al.,
2023](#bib.bib127); [Li et al., 2025b](#bib.bib50); [Gu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib26); [Li et al., 2024a](#bib.bib52)).
Figure [16](#A4.F16 "Figure 16 ‣ Appendix D More Lessons and Opportunities ‣ Memory in the LLM Era: Modular Architectures and Strategies in a Unified Framework [Experiment, Analysis & Benchmark]")
presents a concrete example of this issue. Therefore, we use it as a
complementary metric rather than a primary evaluation metric.

### E.2. F1 and BLEU-1

Token-level F1 measures the token overlap between a generated answer
$`Y`$ and its reference answer $`Y^{*}`$. Specifically, precision,
recall, and F1 are calculated as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (1) |  |
``` math
P=\frac{\left|Y\cap Y^{*}\right|}{|Y|},R=\frac{\left|Y\cap Y^{*}\right|}{|Y^{*}|},\mathrm{F1}=\frac{2PR}{P+R},
``` |  |

where $`\left|Y\cap Y^{*}\right|`$ denotes the number of overlapping
tokens, with repeated tokens counted according to their minimum
occurrence count in the two answers. BLEU-1 measures clipped unigram
precision with a brevity penalty and is calculated as

|     |     |                                                |     |
|-----|-----|------------------------------------------------|-----|
| (2) |     |
             ``` math
             \mathrm{BLEU\mbox{-}1}=\mathrm{BP}\cdot p_{1},
             ```                                             |     |

where

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (3) |  |
``` math
p_{1}=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{w}\min\!\left(\operatorname{Count}_{Y}(w),\operatorname{Count}_{Y^{*}}(w)\right)}{\displaystyle\sum_{w}\operatorname{Count}_{Y}(w)},
``` |  |

and the brevity penalty is defined as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (4) |  |
``` math
\mathrm{BP}=\begin{cases}1,&|Y|\geq|Y^{*}|,\\[2.0pt]
\exp\!\left(1-\dfrac{|Y^{*}|}{|Y|}\right),&|Y|<|Y^{*}|.\end{cases}
``` |  |

Here, $`w`$ denotes a unigram token, and $`\operatorname{Count}_{Y}(w)`$
and $`\operatorname{Count}_{Y^{*}}(w)`$ denote the number of occurrences
of $`w`$ in the generated and reference answers, respectively.

Therefore, F1 and BLEU-1 are sensitive not only to whether the generated
answer contains the correct information, but also to its wording and
verbosity. Additional explanatory content may introduce unmatched tokens
and reduce lexical precision even when the key answer is correct. This
issue is particularly relevant because the official implementations of
different memory methods use different response prompts, resulting in
differences in answer length and style. To reduce this prompt-induced
output-style bias and more accurately compare the information contained
in the answers, we apply the same simplification procedure to the
responses of all methods before computing F1 and BLEU-1.
Table [12](#A5.T12 "Table 12 ‣ E.2. F1 and BLEU-1 ‣ Appendix E Analysis of Evaluation Metrics ‣ Memory in the LLM Era: Modular Architectures and Strategies in a Unified Framework [Experiment, Analysis & Benchmark]")
presents a concrete example illustrating how simplification affects both
metrics, where removing semantically redundant details substantially
increases the scores of the correct response and prevents it from being
ranked below an incorrect but lexically closer answer.
Table [13](#A5.T13 "Table 13 ‣ E.2. F1 and BLEU-1 ‣ Appendix E Analysis of Evaluation Metrics ‣ Memory in the LLM Era: Modular Architectures and Strategies in a Unified Framework [Experiment, Analysis & Benchmark]")
reports the F1 and BLEU-1 scores of different methods before and after
simplification, thereby directly quantifying its impact on the
evaluation results.

## Appendix F Discussion of Method Selection

In this section, we explain the coverage of the selected baselines from
two complementary perspectives: the taxonomy in Memory in the Age of AI
Agents: A Survey ([Hu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib35)) and our four-stage
framework.

Figure 17. Classification and coverage of the evaluated token-level
memory baselines following the taxonomy in Memory in the Age of AI
Agents: A Survey.

Following Memory in the Age of AI Agents: A Survey, which categorizes
agent memory into token-level, parametric, and latent memory, we focus
on text-based token-level memory. Unlike parametric and latent memory,
these methods can be evaluated under the same frozen-LLM setting without
additional training or model modification. Within token-level memory,
the survey further categorizes existing methods into Flat Memory (1D),
Planar Memory (2D), and Hierarchical Memory (3D). As shown in
Figure [17](#A6.F17 "Figure 17 ‣ Appendix F Discussion of Method Selection ‣ Memory in the LLM Era: Modular Architectures and Strategies in a Unified Framework [Experiment, Analysis & Benchmark]"),
for Flat Memory, we select representative methods covering classic
conversational memory (e.g., MemoChat and MemoryBank), widely adopted
designs (e.g., Mem0), efficiency-oriented designs (e.g., LightMem), and
operating-system-inspired memory management (e.g., MemGPT). For Planar
Memory, we include associative memory (e.g., A-MEM),
knowledge-graph-based memory (e.g., Mem0g), tree-structured memory
(e.g., MemTree), and multi-granularity graph memory (e.g., MemGAS). For
Hierarchical Memory, we select representative multi-level designs,
including MemoryOS, MemOS, and the layered temporal graph architecture
Zep.

Beyond this survey-based taxonomy, the selected methods also cover
diverse design choices across all four stages of our framework, as
summarized in
Table [1](#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 1. Introduction ‣ Memory in the LLM Era: Modular Architectures and Strategies in a Unified Framework [Experiment, Analysis & Benchmark]").
Specifically, for information extraction, the selected methods cover
direct archiving at both the message level (e.g., MemoryBank) and
segment level (e.g., MemoryOS), summarization-based extraction (e.g.,
A-MEM), graph-based extraction (e.g., Zep and Mem0g), as well as the
multi-granularity extraction design, MemGAS. For memory management, we
include representative agentic approaches (e.g., Mem0 and LightMem) and
operating-system-inspired approaches (e.g., MemGPT and MemOS). For
memory storage, as shown in
Table [14](#A5.T14 "Table 14 ‣ E.2. F1 and BLEU-1 ‣ Appendix E Analysis of Evaluation Metrics ‣ Memory in the LLM Era: Modular Architectures and Strategies in a Unified Framework [Experiment, Analysis & Benchmark]"),
the selected methods cover representative combinations across both
organization-centric and representation-centric dimensions. For
information retrieval, they cover lexical-based, vector-based, and
structure-based retrieval, as well as hybrid designs that combine
multiple retrieval mechanisms, such as Zep and MemGAS.

## Appendix G Supporting Analysis for the Memory Architecture Selection Roadmap

In this section, we provide the supporting analysis for the memory
architecture selection roadmap. The roadmap covers four major
capabilities of long-term memory systems: Information Persistence,
Memory Association, Temporal Reasoning, and Knowledge Update. These
capabilities are derived from the major QA categories in widely used
benchmarks such as LOCOMO and LONGMEMEVAL. They offer complementary
perspectives on long-term memory requirements and collectively provide
broad coverage of common QA scenarios. The method recommendations are
primarily based on the comprehensive performance of different methods
across LOCOMO and LONGMEMEVAL. When multiple methods achieve comparable
effectiveness but are better suited to different scenarios, we provide
scenario-specific recommendations by further considering factors such as
token consumption and robustness under different noise levels.

For Information Persistence, user-profile scenarios require memory
mechanisms that model and maintain user preferences, as represented by
MemoryBank. For episodic facts involving retrieval of specific
information from historical interactions, MemTree is suitable when
higher token overhead is acceptable, whereas the hierarchical design of
MemoryOS provides a more token-efficient solution.

For Memory Association, the roadmap distinguishes implicit from explicit
associations. Implicit associations, exemplified by LONGMEMEVAL’s
Multi-Session Reasoning tasks, require integrating semantically related
evidence distributed across sessions and levels of abstraction; MemTree
supports this setting through its multi-granular tree organization.
Explicit associations, corresponding to LOCOMO’s Multi-Hop questions,
require multi-hop reasoning over structured paths connecting multiple
memory units, which is supported by MemGAS through its multi-granularity
graph organization.

For Temporal Reasoning, the roadmap distinguishes two representative
types of questions. Time retrieval, mainly represented by the temporal
questions in LOCOMO, focuses on retrieving information associated with a
specific temporal reference. For this type of questions, MemOS achieves
the strongest performance. Time comparison, largely represented by
LONGMEMEVAL’s temporal reasoning tasks, requires comparing temporal
relations among multiple pieces of information. As discussed in
Section 8.2 of our revised paper (Exp.3. Context Scalability Analysis),
increasing context length introduces higher noise levels. Therefore, we
further distinguish low-noise and high-noise settings. Under low-noise
histories, LightMem performs best, while under high-noise histories,
Mem0^(g) achieves more robust performance.

For Knowledge Update, the principal trade-off is between update
effectiveness and token efficiency. MemTree provides better update
performance when substantial update cost is acceptable, whereas the
lightweight update design of LightMem is more appropriate under tight
token budgets.

## Appendix H Memory Construction Cost of Zep

The missing score indicates that Zep did not complete memory
construction on LONGMEMEVAL within two days in our unified experimental
environment. The “fast” performance reported in Zep’s documentation¹¹ 1
[https://www.getzep.com/](https://www.getzep.com/) refers to retrieval
latency, which is separately evaluated in
Table [5](#S8.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 8.2. Evaluation ‣ 8. Experiments ‣ Memory in the LLM Era: Modular Architectures and Strategies in a Unified Framework [Experiment, Analysis & Benchmark]"),
rather than index construction time. In our experiments, Zep exhibits an
average retrieval latency of 536.8 ms, which is higher than the
sub-200 ms latency reported in its documentation. This difference arises
because, to ensure a unified and controlled experimental setting, we use
the open-source implementation released for the Zep paper rather than
its production API, which has undergone multiple subsequent iterations
and optimizations. Regarding index construction, Zep requires several
hours to build the index for LOCOMO under our experimental setting. For
LONGMEMEVAL, whose aggregate text volume is over $`100\times`$ that of
LOCOMO, index construction could not be completed within two days.

To clarify this issue, we further analyze the sources of index
construction overhead. Specifically, Zep represents each message as an
episode and incrementally updates a temporal knowledge graph through
Graphiti²² 2
[https://github.com/getzep/graphiti](https://github.com/getzep/graphiti).
For each episode, it performs entity and fact extraction, entity
resolution, fact deduplication, and conflict handling. As the
conversation grows, the expanding graph increases the candidate space
for these operations, while longer context requires more information to
be processed in LLM prompts. Consequently, later episodes generally
incur higher processing costs, and repeatedly applying this pipeline
over LONGMEMEVAL leads to substantial cumulative construction overhead.
````
